stem:
A 43-year-old man with alcohol-related cirrhosis is admitted for drainage of ascites. Eighteen hours after his last drink he becomes tremulous, sweaty and anxious, with a rising withdrawal score. He usually drinks heavily every day and had a withdrawal seizure two years ago. His albumin is 24 g/L and INR 1.9. He is alert and oriented without asterixis, can swallow, and his breathing is normal; thiamine has been given.

Which medication should the treating doctor use for the withdrawal syndrome?

options.label: A
options.text: Oral diazepam, given as a loading regimen
options.explanation: Diazepam is usually preferred, but in severe liver disease its long half-life and active metabolites accumulate and risk oversedation and precipitating encephalopathy.

options.label: B
options.text: No benzodiazepine, because of his liver disease
options.explanation: He has a past withdrawal seizure and rising scores; withholding benzodiazepines leaves him at risk of seizures and delirium. Liver disease changes the choice of drug, not the need.

options.label: C
options.text: Oral oxazepam, titrated to withdrawal scores
options.explanation: Oxazepam is cleared by glucuronidation with no active metabolites, so it is preferred in severe liver disease. Symptom-triggered dosing against withdrawal scores limits the risk of oversedation.

options.label: D
options.text: Oral olanzapine, titrated to his agitation
options.explanation: Antipsychotics do not prevent withdrawal seizures and lower the seizure threshold. They are adjuncts for agitation or hallucinations, not the treatment for withdrawal.

options.label: E
options.explanation: An infusion of midazolam is for refractory withdrawal in intensive care. He is alert, can swallow and has early withdrawal.

context: Benzodiazepines treat alcohol withdrawal. In severe liver disease, prefer a drug without active metabolites, such as oxazepam, with symptom-triggered dosing.
